findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: no simulation test asserts that any fault was ever injected, so the fault-injecting store can be disconnected from the protocol entirely and the whole file stays green. At CommitProtocolSimulation.java:82 I added `BinStore wired = backing;` and changed line 102 to `tryStart(wired, pod, clock)` -- the FaultInjectingStore is still constructed, still passed nowhere -- and `:sequencer:test` over InvariantsTest + FaultInjectingStoreTest + CommitProtocolSimulationTest was BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 14/14. The two CLEAN tests are unaffected by construction, and `theSameSeedReplaysExactlySoAFailureIsAPermanentRegression` compares `b.faults()` to `a.faults()` -- two EMPTY lists are equal, so ROUGH is the only faulted configuration in the file and it is asserted only against itself. The class javadoc states the opposite in as many words: 'every run asserted clean must FIRST be asserted to have done something: committed, failed over more than once, and actually injected the faults it configured'. The third clause is not asserted anywhere. This is NOT the gap the backlog row defers: the row defers the faulted-run PROGRESS assertions and the seed range because they fail against today's protocol -- I confirmed that is true, see below -- but `assertThat(a.faults()).isNotEmpty()` passes today. Measured: run(99L, 80, 3, ROUGH) injects 85 faults, and every seed 0-59 injects 63-95. One line, no protocol change, closes it.
findings.failure_scenario: A later refactor of `run` -- adding a second overload, threading a CountingBinStore through for M4.9's request assertions, or moving the decorator behind a helper -- wires the raw backing store into `tryStart` and the fault decorator becomes a write-only object. M4.13 then runs 1,000 seeds against an unfaulted store, reports I1-I5 clean, and the milestone's headline claim ('invariants hold across 1,000 deterministic seeds') is established by a suite that injected nothing. That is verbatim the risk M4/SPEC.md:492 names -- 'the simulation proves the simulator' -- and nothing downstream can distinguish it from a real pass.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: the entire fenced-leader ('zombie') subsystem -- lines 86-93, 136-143, 148-165, the `zombies`/`zombiePods` lists and the `zombieWrites` counter -- can be switched off and all three simulation tests pass. I changed line 128 to `if (random.nextBoolean() || true) {` so the zombie branch is never taken; BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 14/14. `Result.zombieWrites()` (line 97, 192) is read by no assertion in the tree. Worse, the CORROBORATING production mutation also survives: I deleted the seal barrier at CommitLog.java:235-241 (`if (sealedAt != null) { throw fenced(sealedAt); }` -- M4.6a's whole subject) and the three simulation tests were BUILD SUCCESSFUL. The comment at lines 86-93 says 'MEASURED -- deleting M4.6a's seal barrier from `recover` entirely left this sweep green' about the version WITHOUT zombies, which reads as a claim that the version WITH them does not; it still does. I also measured why: with the two seeds the tests actually use (7 CLEAN and 99 ROUGH) `zombieWrites == 0`, i.e. no zombie commit ever succeeds, and across seeds 0-59 only 14, 22 and 42 produce a non-zero count -- none of them are tested. So I5, which the comment calls reachable ONLY through a zombie, is not reached by any test in this commit.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone simplifies the harness -- 'pods that lost the lease are dropped, the zombie list is dead weight' is a reasonable-looking cleanup, and the counter it feeds is asserted by nothing -- and the suite stays green. The seal protocol then has no simulation coverage at all: a regression in `CommitLog.commit`'s sealed-chain barrier, or in `recover`'s remembering of `sealedAt`, lets a fenced leader's delta land past the SEAL and be acknowledged (an I5 violation and, via a reader, an I3 one) with 1,000 seeds reporting clean. Concretely: on a real failover the old leader's in-flight commit is acked, the new leader assigns the same offsets, and two OpenSearch replicas under `all_active` diverge -- the exact consequence I2/I5 exist to prevent.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: `putIfMatch`'s ambiguous-write path is unconstrained. I deleted the three lines that land the write (`byte[] bytes = read(b); delegate.putIfMatch(k, new Body(...), v);` at 132-134), leaving the branch as a clean `throw` -- so the fault becomes 'the write never happened' instead of 'the write landed and the response was lost' -- and all 14 tests were BUILD SUCCESSFUL. The only test of this property, `FaultInjectingStoreTest.anAmbiguousPutLANDSWhileReportingFailure`:44, exercises `putIfAbsent` alone. That is the wrong half: `putIfMatch` is the LEASE CAS, and the class javadoc justifies the whole ambiguity machinery by naming three lease defects -- 'M4.3d's self-fencing renew, M4.3g's acquisition, M4.3h's single refresh attempt' -- every one of which lives on `putIfMatch`, not on `putIfAbsent`. The javadoc's headline ('THE AMBIGUOUS WRITE IS THE POINT') is asserted for the method the cited defects do not use.
findings.failure_scenario: The ambiguous-lease-CAS fault silently degrades to a clean failure -- by this mutation, or by a refactor that hoists the `read(b)`/re-body dance into a helper and drops it from one call site. Every LeaseManager ambiguity path then sees only 'the renew failed', never 'the renew succeeded and you were not told'. ADR-0027's accepted bound (one refresh attempt) and the self-fencing-renew class of defect become unreachable by the simulation, and M4.13 reports 1,000 clean seeds for a lease protocol whose hardest case was never generated. Nothing in the tree would show the fault class had weakened.

findings.summary: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED: the I1 predicate can be deleted outright. I replaced lines 84-88 with a bare `seenAt.put(e.sequence(), i);` -- no duplicate detection, no Violation -- and all 14 tests were BUILD SUCCESSFUL. No fixture in InvariantsTest produces a duplicate sequence, so the branch is executed on every chain and constrained on none. That directly contradicts the file's own opening comment ('the weight here is on the chains that MUST be reported -- one per invariant, each hand-built to violate exactly one thing'): there is an I5 fixture, an I2 fixture and a chain-gap fixture, and no I1 fixture. It is cheaply reachable -- `put(store, log, 2, delta(1, ...))` writes an entry whose encoded sequence is 1 into slot 2, which is exactly the corruption the check exists to name. ⚠️ Stated honestly: the SPEC's I1 testable clause ('two writers racing one seq produce exactly one winner') IS covered, by FaultInjectingStoreTest.aDuplicatedPutIsHarmlessBecausePutIfAbsentIsWriteOnce. What is uncovered is the CHECKER that M4.13 will use to report I1 over 1,000 seeds.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 runs 1,000 seeds and reports 'I1-I5 hold'. The I1 clause of that report is unfalsifiable: the branch could have been deleted, could compare the wrong field, or could key `seenAt` on the slot index rather than the decoded sequence, and every seed still comes back clean. A future backend or a change to `CommitLog.keyFor`/`ChainEntry.decode` that lets a sequence number appear twice -- the one thing the class javadoc says I1 is checked for, 'because a backend whose write-once primitive slipped would break I1 with nothing here being wrong' -- passes the simulation silently, and the milestone's completion condition is signed off on a checker that examined it without being able to disagree.

findings.summary: TWO SURVIVING MUTATIONS in `inheritedOffsets`, the 25-line block that decides how much history a successor chain is checked against -- i.e. the sole determinant of whether a cross-epoch I2 is reported. (a) I deleted the step-over loop at 158-162 entirely ('// MUTATION: never step over an unopened chain'): BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 14/14. (b) I changed line 156 to `long upTo = Long.MAX_VALUE;` so the checker over-inherits the predecessor's WHOLE chain rather than stopping at the slot the CONTINUE names: BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 14/14. (b) is the dangerous direction -- it makes the checker inherit offsets from entries written PAST a seal, which is precisely how a genuine I2 gets masked. Under CLEAN faults no chain is ever abandoned mid-open (I swept seeds 0-59: zero violations, and the step-over path is not needed), and InvariantsTest builds no abandoned-chain fixture, so the whole block runs unexercised. ⚠️ NOT a finding, recorded so nobody chases it: `>` -> `>=` at line 167 is an EQUIVALENT mutant -- LocalSequencer.java:94 always passes a Seal's sequence as `prevSeq`, and a Seal contributes no offsets.
findings.failure_scenario: The step-over arithmetic drifts out of step with the protocol -- M4.10's durable `(podId, flushSeq)` or M4.16's burned-epoch fix changes how epochs advance, and the checker's independently-restated rule (line 151-155 says so explicitly: 'if the protocol changes both must move') is not moved. It then walks to the wrong ancestor and inherits either too much or too little. Too much and a real offset rewind is reported clean; too little and every faulted seed reports a spurious I2 and the 1,000-seed run is disabled as noisy. Either way a hand-built two-chain fixture with an abandoned epoch between them would have caught it and none exists.

findings.summary: THE `unreachable` FAULT CLASS IS NOT ASSERTED TO BE OBSERVABLE, contradicting the class javadoc's 'every fault class here is asserted to FIRE and to be OBSERVABLE, not merely configured'. Two surviving mutations, both measured green over all 14 tests: (a) drop `injected.add(new Injected("unreachable", key))` from putIfAbsent's guard at 72, leaving the throw -- the determinism test compares two runs of the SAME mutant so the lists stay equal, and `isNotEmpty` is still satisfied by the ambiguous/duplicate entries; (b) remove the whole unreachable guard from `stat` (106-109), `get` (114-117) and `list` (147-150) at once, so no read path can ever fail. Related and weaker than it reads: FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:90 checks the duplicate fault only with `isNotEmpty()`, so changing the recorded kind string at line 93 from "duplicatePut" to anything else survives; only "ambiguousPut" has its kind pinned (line 64, `containsExactly`).
findings.failure_scenario: Criterion 1 requires each fault class to have a seed where it changes the outcome, 'reported by the harness'. The report is `injected()`. A class that fires but is not recorded, or is recorded under another class's name, makes that report wrong in the direction that looks like success: M4.13 tabulates 'unreachable: 40 occurrences' from entries that were actually duplicates, or tabulates zero and the gap is read as 'this fault class is rare on these seeds' rather than 'this fault class is not wired'. The read-path variant is the bigger hole -- with (b) applied, no LIST or GET in recovery ever fails, so every recovery path in the simulation runs against a store that is only ever unreachable on writes.

findings.summary: WALL CLOCK WHERE THE SEAM EXISTS AND IS IN THIS COMMIT. Lines 60 and 154 pass `java.time.Clock.systemUTC()` to `LeaseManager` with a 10-second TTL, while `SimulatedClock` is added by this same diff, sits in the same package, and is what CommitProtocolSimulation uses for exactly this. testing.md rule 1 and non-negotiable 7 both point the other way, and `LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest`/`IngestTestSupport` already carry a round-1 finding about this precise fixture shape. Note the @Timeout is 60s, so a stall long enough to break the test is not cut short by the timeout first.
findings.failure_scenario: On a loaded or swapping WSL2 box, more than 10 real seconds elapse between `LocalSequencer.start` and the second `commit` in `aTakeoversTWOChainsAreCheckedACROSSTheirJoin`. The first pod's lease expires mid-test, the second pod acquires at a different epoch than the assertion assumes, and the test fails -- or, in the other direction, passes for a reason unrelated to the seal/CONTINUE path it names. Neither outcome is reproducible from the source, and the failure gets triaged as a flake rather than as a defect, which is the exact property the SimulatedClock in this commit was added to buy.

findings.summary: `theCheckerSAYSItNowEXAMINESTheBoundaryBetweenChains` asserts a hardcoded constant. `Invariants.crossEpochOffsetsChecked()` (Invariants.java:67-69) is `return true;` and is derived from nothing, so this test is falsifiable only by editing that literal. It cannot detect the property it claims to guard: I gutted `inheritedOffsets` (`if (true) { return inherited; }` at the top) and this test PASSED -- the mutation was caught by `aTakeoversTWOChainsAreCheckedACROSSTheirJoin` and `aCleanRunViolatesNothing`, both of which failed. So the guarantee is real and is carried by those two, not by this one. Recorded because the comment at 159-164 claims the reverse ('none can catch the checker reporting clean for a property it never looked at. The flag exists so that claim is in the API'), and a reader trusting it would take the flag as the evidence.
findings.failure_scenario: The cross-epoch inheritance is removed or made conditional -- say `inheritedOffsets` returns early for chains deeper than one hop, a plausible shape once M4.9 bounds recovery -- and the flag keeps returning true. This test keeps passing, and its name and message ('a clean report over two chains now says something about the join between them') become false while remaining green. The next author reading the file believes the boundary is self-reporting and does not add the fixture that would actually pin the narrowed case.

findings.summary: THE SWEEP IS ~40x MORE EXPENSIVE THAN IT NEEDS TO BE, which matters because M4.13's stated budget is <60s for 1,000 seeds and this is the loop it will run. Line 183 iterates `epoch <= pods * (long) rounds` (360 epochs for the tested 3 pods x 120 rounds) against at most ~18 chains that exist, and line 188 calls `Invariants.checkChain(backing, PREFIX, epoch)` a SECOND time for the same epoch, discarding the result -- `!checkChain(...).isEmpty() || hasChain(...)` is equivalent to `hasChain(...)` alone, since a violation implies a chain. Each call is a full LIST+GET walk of the chain plus a recursive predecessor walk. Separately, CommitProtocolSimulationTest.java:31 and :45 run the identical `run(7L, 120, 3, CLEAN)` twice.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 scales this to 1,000 seeds, misses the <60s budget, and the response is to cut the seed count or the round count -- a threshold moved in the weakening direction (non-negotiable 2) for a reason that is an accident of this loop rather than a real cost. The duplicated call is also a live trap: it is the kind of line a later reader deletes as dead, and deleting the wrong half of `!checkChain(...).isEmpty() || hasChain(...)` silently changes `highestEpoch`, which IS asserted (CommitProtocolSimulationTest.java:38).
